p.src: The story tells how Duan Jingzhu came running up and said to Lin Chong and the others, “Yang Lin, Shi Yong, and I went north to buy horses. Once there, we selected more than two hundred fine steeds—strong, spirited animals with sound sinews and excellent coats—and bought them; but on our way back, when we reached the Qingzhou region, a band of outlaws robbed us of every horse. Their leader was Yu Baosi, known as the ‘Perilous-Road God,’ and he had gathered more than two hundred men. They delivered all the horses to Zengtou Market. I do not know what became of Shi Yong and Yang Lin. I escaped through the night and came here to report what happened.” When Guan Sheng heard this, he told them to return to the stronghold first, meet their elder brother, and then discuss the matter. They all crossed the water and went to the Hall of Loyalty and Righteousness, where they met Song Jiang. Guan Sheng presented Shan Tinggui and Wei Dingguo, who exchanged greetings with every leader, great and small. Li Kui then recounted how, after descending the mountain and killing Han Bolong, he had met Jiao Ting and Bao Xu and gone with them to take Lingzhou. When Song Jiang had heard the whole account, he rejoiced that four more worthy heroes had joined them. Duan Jingzhu gave a full account of the stolen horses. On hearing it, Song Jiang flew into a rage and said, “They stole our horses before, and now they have treated us outrageously yet again. King Chao’s wrong remains unavenged, and it gives me no peace day or night. If we do not avenge him, we shall become a laughingstock.” Wu Yong said, “The spring weather has now turned warm, making this the perfect time to fight. When we advanced against them before, the terrain was against us. This time we must win through strategy.” Song Jiang said, “This hatred has sunk into my very marrow. I swear I shall not return to the mountain until it is avenged.” Wu Yong said, “Let us first send Shi Qian. He can fly over eaves and run along walls, so he can go there, gather intelligence, and report back. Then we shall decide what to do.” Shi Qian accepted the order and departed. Within two or three days, Yang Lin and Shi Yong escaped back to the stronghold. They reported in full how Shi Wengong of Zengtou Market had boasted that he and the Marsh of Mount Liang could never coexist. As soon as Song Jiang heard this, he wanted to raise the army. Wu Yong said, “It will not be too late to march after Shi Qian returns with his report.” But Song Jiang’s breast was filled with fury, and he was so intent on vengeance that he could not endure even a moment’s delay. He also sent Dai Zong flying off to investigate and ordered him to return with an immediate report.

p.src: Only a few days later, Dai Zong returned first and reported, “Zengtou Market means to avenge Lingzhou and is preparing to mobilize its troops. It has now established a great camp at the entrance to the town and set up its central command in Fahua Temple. Banners have been planted everywhere for hundreds of li, and there is no telling by which road we can advance.” The next day, Shi Qian returned to the stronghold and reported, “I went right inside Zengtou Market and learned all the particulars. They have now established five fortified camps. At the front of Zengtou Market, more than two thousand men guard the village entrance. The chief camp is commanded by the instructor Shi Wengong. The northern camp is held by Zeng Tu and the assistant instructor Su Ding; the southern by the second son, Zeng Mi; the western by the third son, Zeng Suo; the eastern by the fourth son, Zeng Kui; and the central by the fifth son, Zeng Sheng, together with his father, Zeng Nong. This Yu Baosi of Qingzhou stands ten feet tall and measures several spans around the waist. He is nicknamed the ‘Perilous-Road God,’ and he is keeping and feeding all the stolen horses inside Fahua Temple.”

p.src: When Wu Yong had heard the report, he ordered all the commanders to assemble and discussed the matter with them: “Since they have set up five fortified camps, we shall divide our forces into five armies and attack their five camps by five separate routes.” Lu Junyi rose and said, “I was fortunate enough to have my life saved and to be brought to the mountain, yet I have done nothing to repay that kindness. Now I wish to risk my life in the vanguard. What is your honored opinion?” Song Jiang was delighted and said, “If you are willing to descend the mountain, Master Lu, you shall command the vanguard.” Wu Yong remonstrated, “Master Lu has only just arrived at the stronghold and has not yet seen battle. The mountain paths are rugged and difficult to traverse on horseback, so he must not serve as the forward vanguard. Let him lead a separate force and lie in ambush on level ground. When he hears the cannon from the central army, he can come forward to support us.” Wu Yong’s true concern was that if Lu Junyi captured Shi Wengong, Song Jiang would honor Chao Gai’s dying words and yield the leadership to him. For that reason, he would not appoint Lu to command the forward vanguard. Song Jiang, for his part, wanted only for Lu Junyi to win distinction, so that he might take this opportunity to make him master of the stronghold. Wu Yong refused to allow it and firmly ordered Master Lu to take Yan Qing and lead five hundred infantrymen to await the signal on a small road across the level ground. The troops were then divided among five routes. To attack the main camp directly south of Zengtou Market, the cavalry leaders Qin Ming, the ‘Thunderbolt,’ and Hua Rong, the ‘Lesser Li Guang,’ were assigned three thousand troops, with Ma Lin and Deng Fei as their deputies; to attack the main camp directly east of Zengtou Market, the infantry leaders Lu Zhishen, the ‘Flowery Monk,’ and Wu Song, the ‘Pilgrim,’ were assigned three thousand troops, with Kong Ming and Kong Liang as their deputies; to attack the main camp directly north of Zengtou Market, the cavalry leaders Yang Zhi, the ‘Blue-Faced Beast,’ and Shi Jin, the ‘Nine-Dragoned,’ were assigned three thousand troops, with Yang Chun and Chen Da as their deputies; to attack the main camp directly west of Zengtou Market, the infantry leaders Zhu Tong, the ‘Lord of the Beautiful Beard,’ and Lei Heng, the ‘Winged Tiger,’ were assigned three thousand troops, with Zou Yuan and Zou Run as their deputies; to attack the central headquarters of Zengtou Market, the supreme leader Song Gongming and the military advisers Wu Yong and Gongsun Sheng were assigned five thousand troops, accompanied by the deputy commanders Lü Fang, Guo Sheng, Xie Zhen, Xie Bao, Dai Zong, and Shi Qian; and to unite the rear, the infantry leaders Li Kui, the ‘Black Whirlwind,’ and Fan Rui, the ‘Demon King Who Roils the World,’ together with the deputy commanders Xiang Chong and Li Gun, were given five thousand cavalrymen and infantrymen. All the remaining leaders were to guard the stronghold.

p.src: We shall leave aside Song Jiang leading the troops and commanders of the five armies in their great advance. Meanwhile, the scouts of Zengtou Market learned every detail and reported back to the stronghold. When Chief Zeng heard the report, he summoned the instructors Shi Wengong and Su Ding to discuss this grave military situation. Shi Wengong said, “When the Liangshan Marsh forces come, we must make ample use of pitfalls; only then can we capture their fierce soldiers and valiant commanders. Against this band of outlaws, that stratagem must be our best policy.” Chief Zeng ordered the villagers to take hoes and iron spades, dig scores of pitfalls at the village entrance, and cover them loosely with earth. Troops were placed in ambush on every side, awaiting the enemy’s arrival. They also dug more than a dozen pitfalls on the northern road into Zengtou Market. Before Song Jiang’s forces set out, Wu Yong secretly sent Shi Qian ahead once more to gather intelligence. Several days later Shi Qian returned and reported, “South and north of the Zengtou Market stronghold, they have dug countless pitfalls and are merely waiting for our forces to arrive.” Hearing this, Wu Yong laughed loudly. “Nothing remarkable about that!” He led the army onward until it drew near Zengtou Market. At about noon, the vanguard saw a horse approaching, with bronze bells around its neck and pheasant feathers tied to its tail; its rider wore a blue headcloth and white robe and carried a short spear. When the vanguard saw him, they made to give chase, but Wu Yong stopped them. He ordered the army to encamp there, dig a moat on every side, and lay iron caltrops. He then commanded each of the five armies to pitch its own camp separately, likewise digging moats and laying caltrops. For three days after they settled in, Zengtou Market sent no one out to fight. Wu Yong again sent Shi Qian, disguised as a lowly ambush soldier, into the Zengtou Market stronghold to discover why they would not come out. He was also to memorize secretly the positions of all the pitfalls, their distance from the stronghold, and their total number. Shi Qian spent a day there, learned every detail, secretly left marks, and returned to report to the strategist. The next day, Wu Yong issued orders for every man in the infantry vanguard to carry an iron hoe and divide into two columns. He also loaded more than a hundred provision carts with reeds and dry firewood and concealed them in the central army. That evening he ordered the commanders in every camp that at the hour of the Snake next day, they were to wait until the infantry on the eastern and western routes first assaulted the forts. Yang Zhi and Shi Jin, assigned to attack the northern fort of Zengtou Market, were to draw up their cavalry in a single line; even if drums thundered and banners waved there in a feigned display of strength, they were under no circumstances to advance. Wu Yong thus completed the issuing of his orders.

p.src: Now Shi Wengong of Zengtou Market was intent on luring Song Jiang’s forces into attacking the stronghold, where they would fall into the pitfalls. With the road before the fort so narrow, where could they flee? At the hour of the Snake next day, a cannon sounded before the stronghold, and a great body of pursuing troops gathered at the southern gate. Soon afterward, a messenger came from the eastern fort: “A monk is brandishing an iron monk’s staff, and a pilgrim is whirling a pair of戒刀. They are attacking us from front and rear!” Shi Wengong said, “Those two must be Lu Zhishen and Wu Song of Liangshan Marsh.” Fearing that something might go wrong, he detached men to reinforce Zeng Kui. Then another messenger came from the western fort: “A huge long-bearded man and a tiger-faced outlaw are attacking fiercely. Their banners name them ‘Lord of the Beautiful Beard’ Zhu Tong and ‘Winged Tiger’ Lei Heng.” On hearing this, Shi Wengong again detached men, this time to reinforce Zeng Suo. Another cannon sounded before the stronghold, but Shi Wengong held his troops motionless. He meant to wait until the enemy came forward and collapsed the pitfalls, whereupon the ambushers behind the hill would rise together, support the attack, and seize them. Wu Yong, however, sent the cavalry around by two routes behind the hill to sweep toward the front of the stronghold. The infantry in front merely kept watch on the fort and dared not advance; the ambushing troops on both sides had all formed up before the stronghold; then Wu Yong’s forces charged up from behind and drove every one of them into the pits. Just as Shi Wengong was about to come out, Wu Yong pointed with the tip of his whip. A gong sounded in the army camp, and more than a hundred carts were rolled out together and all set ablaze. The reeds, dry firewood, sulfur, and saltpeter upon them all caught at once, and smoke and flame filled the sky. By the time Shi Wengong’s troops came out, the burning carts had formed a barrier across their path. They had no choice but to recoil and hurriedly prepare to withdraw. Gongsun Sheng was already in the formation. Waving his sword, he performed a spell and summoned a great wind, which swept the flames into the southern gate and soon burned the enemy tower and palisades to the ground. Having already won the victory, they sounded the gong and recalled the troops. They returned to their camps on every side and rested there for the night. Shi Wengong repaired the stronghold gates through the night and secured both sides.

p.src: The next day, Zeng Tu conferred with Shi Wengong, saying, “Unless we first behead the leader of the outlaws, it will be difficult to pursue and destroy them.” He charged the instructor Shi Wengong to guard the stockade securely. Zeng Tu led out his soldiers, donned his armor, mounted his horse, and rode forth to challenge the enemy. When Song Jiang learned in the central army that Zeng Tu had issued a challenge, he took Lü Fang and Guo Sheng with him and went forward to the vanguard. Seeing Zeng Tu beyond the command banner, he recalled their old enmity and pointed with his whip. “Who will be the first to seize this wretch for me and avenge our former grievance?” “Little Marquis Wen” Lü Fang spurred his mount, leveled the decorated halberd in his hand, and charged straight at Zeng Tu. The two horses met, their weapons rose together, and they fought for more than thirty bouts. From beneath the command banner, Guo Sheng saw that one of the two combatants was on the verge of defeat. In truth, Lü Fang’s skill was no match for Zeng Tu’s. Even before thirty bouts he was barely holding his own; after thirty, his halberd technique fell into disorder, and he could do no more than parry and dodge. Fearing that harm would befall Lü Fang, Guo Sheng urged his mount into a gallop, gripped his decorated halberd, and flew out from the formation to attack Zeng Tu from the other side. The three horsemen became entangled in a whirling melee before the lines. Now each of the two halberds had a golden leopard’s tail tied to it. Lü Fang and Guo Sheng sought to capture Zeng Tu and raised both halberds together. Quick-eyed Zeng Tu swept them aside with a single stroke of his spear, but the two leopard tails became entangled with its red tassel. They could not wrench them apart, and all three struggled to pull their weapons free for use. “Little Li Guang” Hua Rong saw this from within the formation and feared that the two men would be defeated. He galloped out, raised his carved bow in his left hand, swiftly drew a pointed arrow with his right, set it to the string, pulled the bow to the full, and shot at Zeng Tu. At that very moment Zeng Tu managed to wrench his spear free, while the two halberds remained entangled with each other. It happened in a flash: the instant Zeng Tu freed his spear, he thrust it straight at the base of Lü Fang’s neck. But Hua Rong’s arrow arrived first and struck Zeng Tu squarely in the left arm. He toppled backward from his horse, his helmet inverted and his feet kicking at empty air. Lü Fang and Guo Sheng struck together with their halberds, and Zeng Tu met a violent death. More than a dozen cavalrymen galloped back to inform Shi Wengong, who relayed the news to the central stronghold. When Chief Zeng heard it, he wept bitterly.

p.src: At this, a warrior standing nearby named Zeng Sheng flew into a rage. His martial skill was unsurpassed, and he wielded a pair of flying knives that no man dared approach. Hearing this, he gnashed his teeth in fury and shouted, “Saddle my horse! I will avenge my elder brother!” Commandant Zeng could not restrain him. Fully armed, he snatched up his saber, mounted his horse, and rode straight for the forward stockade. Shi Wengong met him and urged, “Young General, you must not underestimate the enemy. Song Jiang’s army contains many commanders of exceptional wisdom, courage, and valor. In my humble opinion, we should hold our five stockades firmly while secretly sending a man to Lingzhou to make an urgent report to the court. Let it dispatch troops and appoint commanders, greatly reinforcing the government army and dividing it into two forces: one to attack Liangshan Marsh and the other to defend Zengtou Market. The outlaws will then lose the will to remain in battle, withdraw their army, and hurry back to their mountain stronghold. Then, unworthy though I am, I shall pursue and destroy them together with you brothers, and we shall surely win great merit.” Before he had finished speaking, Su Ding, the deputy instructor of the northern stockade, arrived. On hearing the proposal to stand fast, he too said, “Wu Yong of Liangshan Marsh is exceedingly cunning and full of schemes. We must not underestimate the enemy, but should withdraw and hold our defenses. When reinforcements arrive, we can deliberate carefully.” Zeng Sheng cried, “They killed my own brother! p.src: That night the sky was clear, the moon bright, the wind still, and the clouds at rest. In the stockade, Shi Wengong said to Zeng Sheng, “The outlaws lost two commanders today and must surely be afraid. Now is the perfect time to take advantage of their weakness and raid their camp.” Hearing this, Zeng Sheng ordered that Su Ding from the northern stockade, Zeng Mi from the southern stockade, and Zeng Suo from the western stockade bring their troops to join in the raid. Around the second watch, they secretly sent out scouts, removed the bells from their horses, and dressed the men in light armor. They went straight into Song Jiang’s central camp, but found no one anywhere and realized they had raided an empty camp. Crying that they had fallen into a trap, they wheeled about and fled. From the left rushed Double-Headed Serpent Xie Zhen, and from the right Double-Tailed Scorpion Xie Bao; behind them came Little Li Guang Hua Rong in close pursuit. In the darkness, Zeng Suo was thrust from his horse by a stroke of Xie Zhen’s steel fork. Fires were set, battle cries rose from the rear camp, and troops attacked the stockade palisades from both east and west. After fighting in confusion for half the night, Shi Wengong forced a path through and escaped back.

Since the Zeng family has sent a messenger to seek peace, how can we sacrifice the greater cause merely because of a moment’s anger?” He immediately wrote a reply and gave the messenger ten taels of silver as a reward. The messenger returned to his own stockade and presented the letter. When Commandant Zeng and Shi Wengong opened it, they read: “Song Jiang, chief commander of Liangshan Marsh, writes this reply before the tent of Zeng Nong, master of Zengtou Market: A state governs all under Heaven through good faith; a general secures the outer realm through valor. What can a man accomplish without propriety? Wealth obtained without righteousness we shall not take. Liangshan Marsh and Zengtou Market have never borne each other any grudge, but formerly kept within their respective bounds. Yet your commanders committed a moment’s evil and thereby provoked a feud that has lasted years. If you desire peace, you must return the horses seized on both occasions, hand over Yu Baosi, the villain who stole them, and provide gold and silk to reward our soldiers. Let your sincerity be steadfast, and do not slight the proper courtesies. Should you alter your terms, we shall make a different decision.”

p.src: That evening, Shi Wengong set out with Su Ding, Zeng Mi, and Zeng Kui, mobilizing all their forces. The moonlight was hazy that night, and the stars were dim. Shi Wengong and Su Ding led the van, with Zeng Mi and Zeng Kui bringing up the rear. The bells were removed from the horses, and the men wore soft armor as they advanced together upon Song Jiang’s main camp. They saw that the camp gates stood open, that not a soul was inside, and that there was not the slightest movement. Realizing they had fallen into a trap, they immediately turned back. As they hurried back toward their own camp, gongs and drums suddenly sounded within Zengtou Market. Shi Qian had climbed the bell tower of Fahua Temple and begun ringing the bell as a signal. Cannon fire erupted simultaneously at the eastern and western gates, and a tremendous battle cry arose as an unknown multitude of troops stormed in. Meanwhile, inside Fahua Temple, Li Kui, Fan Rui, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun rose together and fought their way out. When Shi Wengong and the others hurried back to the stronghold, they could no longer find the way. Chief Zeng saw the great turmoil within the stronghold and heard that the Liangshan Marsh army was attacking from two directions. There in the stronghold, he hanged himself. Zeng Mi made straight for the western camp, but Zhu Tong thrust him through with a broad-bladed saber and killed him. When Zeng Kui tried to flee to the eastern camp, he was trampled into the mud by horses amid the chaotic fighting. Su Ding fled desperately through the northern gate, only to find countless pitfalls before him. Lu Zhishen and Wu Song came killing in pursuit from behind, while Yang Zhi and Shi Jin blocked him ahead; amid a hail of arrows, Su Ding was shot dead. The men and horses charging up behind all plunged into the pitfalls, piling one atop another; none could tell how many perished there.

The moonlight was hazy that night, and the stars were dim.

Shi Wengong and Su Ding led the van, with Zeng Mi and Zeng Kui bringing up the rear. The bells were removed from the horses, and the men wore soft armor as they advanced together upon Song Jiang’s main camp.
They saw that the camp gates stood open, that not a soul was inside, and that there was not the slightest movement. Realizing they had fallen into a trap, they immediately turned back.

As they hurried back toward their own camp, gongs and drums suddenly sounded within Zengtou Market. Shi Qian had climbed the bell tower of Fahua Temple and begun ringing the bell as a signal. Cannon fire erupted simultaneously at the eastern and western gates, and a tremendous battle cry arose as an unknown multitude of troops stormed in.
Meanwhile, inside Fahua Temple, Li Kui, Fan Rui, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun rose together and fought their way out.
When Shi Wengong and the others hurried back to the stronghold, they could no longer find the way.
Chief Zeng saw the great turmoil within the stronghold and heard that the Liangshan Marsh army was attacking from two directions. There in the stronghold, he hanged himself.
Zeng Mi made straight for the western camp, but Zhu Tong thrust him through with a broad-bladed saber and killed him.
When Zeng Kui tried to flee to the eastern camp, he was trampled into the mud by horses amid the chaotic fighting.

Su Ding fled desperately through the northern gate, only to find countless pitfalls before him. Lu Zhishen and Wu Song came killing in pursuit from behind, while Yang Zhi and Shi Jin blocked him ahead; amid a hail of arrows, Su Ding was shot dead.
The men and horses charging up behind all plunged into the pitfalls, piling one atop another; none could tell how many perished there.

p.src: Now Shi Wengong had obtained this thousand-li steed. Swiftly it bore him out through the western gate, and he fled into the wilderness. By then, black mist shrouded the sky, and he could no longer tell north from south. After riding some twenty-odd li, he had no idea where he was; suddenly gongs rang out in unison behind the woods, and four or five hundred soldiers charged forth. At their head was an officer wielding a staff, who struck straight at the horse's legs. But the horse was a dragon colt capable of a thousand li; when the staff came at it, it leapt clean over the man's head. As Shi Wengong raced on, he saw dark clouds slowly gathering, felt the chill wind whistle, and watched black mist billow and a gale rage; then a figure appeared in midair and barred his way. Thinking it some divine warrior, Shi Wengong reined about, but whichever way he turned—east, west, south, or north—Chao Gai's vengeful spirit haunted and obstructed him. Shi Wengong doubled back along the old road, only to run into Yan Qing, the Prodigal, while Lu Junyi, the Jade Qilin, wheeled around and shouted, “You vicious brigand! Where do you think you're going?” With a single thrust of his broad-bladed sword into Shi Wengong's thigh, Lu Junyi knocked him from the saddle. They bound him with ropes and escorted him back to Zengtou Market. Yan Qing led away the thousand-li dragon colt and went straight to the main camp. At the sight, Song Jiang felt both joy and anger: joy that Squire Lu had won such merit, and anger from his hatred of Shi Wengong for shooting and killing Heavenly King Chao. When a man meets his mortal enemy, his eyes blaze all the fiercer. They first beheaded Zeng Sheng there and then, and spared not one member of the Zeng household, old or young. All the gold, silver, valuables, rice, wheat, and provisions they had seized were loaded onto carts and taken back to Liangshan Marsh, there to be distributed among the various commanders and used to reward the entire army. Meanwhile, Guan Sheng had led his troops in driving back the Qingzhou forces, while Hua Rong had led his men in scattering the Lingzhou army; both now returned. Not one commander, great or small, was missing. They had also gained the thousand-li dragon colt known as the Night-Illuminating Jade Lion; the rest of the spoils need not be recounted. They imprisoned Shi Wengong in a caged cart, put the troops and horses in order, and set off for Liangshan Marsh. They caused no disturbance in any prefecture, county, village, or hamlet along the way. Upon returning to the stronghold, they assembled in the Hall of Loyalty and Righteousness to pay homage to Chao Gai's spirit. Song Jiang gave orders for Xiao Rang, the Master Calligrapher, to compose a funeral oration. Every commander, high and low, donned mourning and lamented, and they cut open Shi Wengong's belly and tore out his heart. When the sacrifice to Chao Gai was concluded, Song Jiang conferred with his brothers in the Hall of Loyalty and Righteousness about choosing the lord of Liangshan Marsh.

p.src: Wu Yong said, “Elder Brother should hold the highest place, Squire Lu the second, and all the other brothers should retain their former ranks.” Song Jiang replied, “Before his death, Heavenly King Chao declared: ‘Whoever captures Shi Wengong, no matter who he may be, shall become lord of Liangshan Marsh.’ Today Squire Lu captured the villain alive, brought him to the mountain as an offering to Brother Chao, and avenged his death. He rightfully deserves the highest place; no more need be said.” Lu Junyi said, “Your younger brother is poor in virtue and scant in talent. How could I dare accept this position? Even to occupy the lowest rank would be more than I deserve.” Song Jiang said, “It is not from excessive modesty that I speak. There are three respects in which I am inferior to you, Squire. First, I, Song Jiang, am short and dark, plain-featured and untalented; you, Squire, are dignified in appearance and imposing in bearing, with the countenance of a nobleman. Second, I began as a petty clerk, became a fugitive after committing a crime, and only through the brothers' kindness in not rejecting me do I temporarily occupy this honored place; you were born into a wealthy and noble household and have long enjoyed renown as a hero. Though you have met with some grave dangers, Heaven has repeatedly protected you. Third, in civil affairs I cannot bring peace to the realm, nor in war can I win the allegiance of the people. My hands lack even the strength to bind a chicken, and I have not an inch's worth of martial achievement to my name; you possess strength enough to face ten thousand men and are deeply versed in both ancient and present learning. Who under Heaven would not submit at the mere report of your coming? With such talent and virtue, honored brother, you are precisely the man who should become lord of this stronghold. If someday we submit to the imperial court, establish great merit, and rise in rank and title, you will be able to bring honor to all the brothers. My mind is made up. You must not refuse.” Lu Junyi bowed to the floor and said, “Elder Brother, you speak all this in vain. I, Lu, would sooner die; truly, I cannot obey.” Wu Yong urged, “If Elder Brother holds the highest place and Squire Lu the second, everyone will accept it. If Elder Brother continues yielding the position again and again, I fear you will dishearten everyone.” In fact, Wu Yong had already signaled the others with his eyes, and that was why he spoke these words. Then Li Kui, the Black Whirlwind, shouted, “Back in Jiangzhou I risked my life and followed you here, and everyone has always yielded pride of place to you. I don't fear even Heaven itself! Why the devil do you keep yielding back and forth? I'll start killing right now, and then we can all go our separate ways!” Wu Song saw Wu Yong signaling the others with his eyes and also burst out, “Many of the officers under Elder Brother have received commissions from the imperial court, yet even they yield to Elder Brother. How could they consent to follow anyone else?” Liu Tang said, “When the seven of us first came up the mountain, even then we meant to place Elder Brother above us. And today you would yield the position to someone else!” Lu Zhishen bellowed, “If Elder Brother still means to yield to someone else, we shall each go our own way!” Song Jiang said, “All of you need say no more. I have a plan of my own. We shall leave it entirely to Heaven's will, see what comes of it, and only then make our decision.” Wu Yong said, “Whatever your excellent proposal may be, please tell us.” Song Jiang replied, “There are two matters.” Indeed, these would bring two more heroes into Liangshan Marsh, and stir up yet another calamity in Dongping Prefecture. It would bring every last Heavenly Spirit into the stronghold, and gather the whole company of Earthly Fiends beside the marsh. But what were the two matters Song Jiang proposed? Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
